dialog.body: Public Works storm line, this is Lorraine. What can I help you with this afternoon?

Hi. My name is Marie Pucci. I'm calling about the storm drain at the corner by 701 Thames Street, in the Fifth Ward. I know City Hall is closed today. I figured this line was the only thing open on a Sunday, so I'm using it.
That's what it's here for, so you're fine. Okay, Marie Pucci, 701 Thames Street, Fifth Ward. And it's the storm drain at the corner. Is it backing up right now, or is this about the rain we just had?

The rain we just had. Friday into Saturday. It's not backing up right now. It's drained down. But it overflowed again. The catch basin filled up and came up over the curb onto the sidewalk, and then the street ponded. It came all the way up to the top step of the house.
Up to the top step. Okay. And that was Friday night?

Friday night into Saturday morning. I was up all night watching it. I had the pump down by the door, plugged in, hose run out to the back, ready to go. I sat by the window and watched the water come up the sidewalk. I didn't sleep.
Oh, that's a long night. Did any water get inside the house this time?

No. The basement stayed dry this time. Which is the only reason I'm calling on a Sunday instead of Saturday at six in the morning. But I want it on the record that it's dry because we got lucky, not because anything got fixed. The basement already flooded twice this winter. Once after the coastal storm in January, and again after the nor'easter at the end of February. Two times. This was going to be three.

Okay. So twice this winter, January and late February, and this time it stayed dry, but the water came right up to the top step. I'm going to pull up the address and see what we've got. Give me one second. [pause] Okay, 701 Thames. Yeah, there's a history here. I see a call in January, Saturday the tenth, that was... Paul Pucci?
My husband. Yes. His mother owns the house. Eleanor. We live there with her.
Okay. So Paul called on the tenth, and then I see a call from you on the twelfth, January twelfth.

Right. That was after the crew came and cleared off the grate. They took the leaves off the top and left. Nothing under the street. I called that day and said the problem is under the street, the pipe, not the leaves. Nobody came back after that. Then it flooded again in February.
I see that. Then there's a call from Eleanor on February twenty-fourth, and Paul again on the twenty-fifth, and then a crew went out Thursday the twenty-sixth.

Yes. They jetted the line. They told us the pipe under the corner needs a camera inspection. Then a supervisor called Eleanor the next day and said engineering would review the corner. That was the twenty-seventh. That's more than a week ago. So my question is what came of that. Did anybody put a camera down there. Did engineering look at it. Because nobody has told us anything, and it overflowed again.

Okay, let me read what's on here so I'm telling you exactly what I see. Thursday, February twenty-sixth, crew jetted the line at the corner, recommended a camera inspection of the pipe under the corner. Friday the twenty-seventh, supervisor contacted Eleanor Pucci, engineering to review. And... [pause] that's the last entry. I don't see an inspection date on here. Nothing scheduled for the camera yet.
Nothing scheduled.
Not that I can see, no.

Okay. So that's the same as January. Somebody comes out, does one thing, says somebody else needs to do the real thing, and then it sits. I'm not yelling at you. I know you're answering the phone on a Sunday. But this is the third storm in a row where that corner floods, and every time the answer is somebody's going to look at it.

No, I hear you. And you're right that it's sitting there with no date on it. What I can do today is put a note on this, that it overflowed again with this rain, water to the top step, and that the camera inspection still hasn't been scheduled, and send it to the supervisor to follow up with you directly. Not just the general queue.

Okay. Yes. Do that. And there's one more thing they should know. I went out and looked at the grate this morning. It's half full. Sand and trash. Somebody's coffee cup, bags, a lot of sand. Probably from the road and whatever washed down from the hill. Half the grate is covered. So even if the pipe was fine, the water can't get in fast enough.
Half full of sand and trash. Okay, I'm putting that in. Grate at the corner half blocked with sand and debris as of Sunday morning. That one, at least, is a quick thing for a crew to clean out.
They cleaned it in January. It filled back up. That's sort of the point.
Understood. I'm noting that it's refilled since it was cleared.

And I want to ask about something else. Next time there's a big storm coming, can the city put a pump truck on that corner. Just park it there while it's raining and pump the water out before it gets to the houses. Because I can't sit up every night with a pump by the door. And that's just our house. The neighbors have the same water out front.

A pump truck staged at the corner during the next storm. That's not something I can book from here, honestly. That would be up to the supervisor and whoever's running the storm crews that night. But I can put the request in the note, clearly, so it's in front of them. Do you want me to word it as a request for the next forecasted storm?
Yes. Word it like that. The next storm. Before it starts, not after it's already in the street.
Okay. 'Resident requests a pump truck be staged at the corner by 701 Thames ahead of the next forecasted storm, before the rain starts.' That sound right?
That's right.
Okay. Now the supervisor called Eleanor last time. Do you want the follow-up to go to Eleanor again, or to you?
To me. Eleanor works during the week, she's at the front desk all day, she can't really pick up. I'm easier to get. My cell is 401-555-0161.
Let me read that back. 401-555-0161, Marie Pucci, cell.
Yes.
Okay. And I'm going to give you a reference number for this note so if you call back you can just give them that and they'll pull it right up. You have something to write with?
Go ahead.
It's S-D, as in storm drain, dash, two six, dash, zero three zero eight four one seven.
S-D, two six, zero three zero eight four seven one.
Close. It's four one seven at the end, not four seven one. So S-D, two six, zero three zero eight, four one seven.
Four one seven. Okay. I wrote it wrong. S-D, two six, zero three zero eight four one seven.
That's it. You got it.
Is that a new number, or is it tied to the other calls? Because last time Paul said it was like starting over every time somebody called.

It's a new note, but it's on the same address record. Everything from January on is attached to 701 Thames, so whoever opens it sees the whole history, the January grate cleaning, the jetting, the supervisor call, and now this.
Okay. Because the history is the problem. Anyone who looks at it should be able to see it's the same corner every time.
It's all right there. I'll put a line at the top of the note that says repeat location, so it's the first thing they read.
Thank you. And when is somebody going to call me. Realistically.

The office opens back up tomorrow morning, and the supervisors go through the weekend storm-line notes first thing Monday. So I'd say tomorrow or Tuesday you should hear something. If it gets to Wednesday and nobody's reached out, call the main Public Works number during the day and give them that reference.
Okay. Tomorrow or Tuesday. And if they say engineering is still reviewing, what do I say to that.

Ask them for a date for the camera inspection. That's the concrete thing. The crew already said it needs one. Ask when it's on the schedule. If they don't have one, ask who does, and ask them to call you once it's set.

A date for the camera. Okay. I'll ask that. [pause] I just want to say, we've been patient. Eleanor's been in that house almost forty years. She says it never used to do this. Now it's every storm. We get the furniture up, we get the shelves up, we shut breakers off, we sit up. And then we call and we get told somebody will look. I'm tired of that answer.

That's fair. And I'm not going to tell you it'll be fixed by the next storm, because I don't know that. But the note's going straight to the supervisor with the date problem spelled out, the grate, and the pump truck request. That's the strongest thing I can do from this phone on a Sunday.
Okay. I understand that. Can you read me what the note says. All of it. So I know what they're getting.

Sure. 'Repeat location. 701 Thames Street, Fifth Ward, corner catch basin. Caller Marie Pucci, daughter-in-law of owner Eleanor Pucci, cell 401-555-0161. Catch basin overflowed onto the sidewalk again during the Friday into Saturday rain, street ponded to the top step. Resident watched overnight with a pump ready. Basement stayed dry this event; basement flooded twice previously this winter, January and late February. Grate at the corner currently about half full of sand and trash, refilled since January cleaning. Crew on February twenty-sixth jetted the line and recommended a camera inspection; no inspection date scheduled as of today. Requesting supervisor follow-up with a date for the camera inspection. Also requesting a pump truck be staged at the corner ahead of the next forecasted storm.' And then the reference number.
That's everything. Okay. Thank you for reading it.
Of course. Anything else going on out there right now? Any water still standing?
No. It's down. There's a line of sand on the sidewalk where it was. That's all.
Okay. If it starts backing up again before anybody calls you, use this line, any hour, and tell them it's an active backup at a repeat location. They'll move it up.
Okay. I'll do that. Thanks, Lorraine.
You're welcome, Marie. Go get some sleep tonight.
I'll try. Bye.
